title: How Atomisation Fixed My Step-by-Step Lethal Mutation and Recharged My Teaching
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: After more than a decade in the secondary classroom, Dario Emanuele describes how Kris Boulton's Atomisation framework has fundamentally altered his professional identity as a teacher. His central metaphor is the X-ray: atomisation gives the teacher the ability to see through the surface procedure of a topic and identify the thirty or more independent conceptual atoms beneath it, creating a precise map of what must be mastered and in what sequence. He warns against the 'lethal mutation' of treating true atomisation as mere step-by-step instruction, which produces fragile procedural scripts that collapse when a question format shifts. He then identifies three practical wins: slowing down at the atomic level creates speed later, atomised resources become universal across ability groups, and atomic-level question design turns mini-whiteboard feedback into scalpel-precise diagnosis of exactly which cognitive link has failed.
points: The X-ray metaphor: atomisation lets teachers see through a surface procedure to the thirty-plus conceptual atoms beneath it, mapping prerequisite knowledge for sequencing and diagnosis.
The lethal mutation of step-by-step instruction teaches procedure but not concept, so the script breaks when the problem format changes even slightly.
Slowing down to automate each atom feels counterproductive but pays off: students later handle complex problems independently because the foundations require no cognitive effort.
Atomised lessons make differentiated materials unnecessary because the atoms are the same for all groups; only the rate of progression varies.
Atomic-level question design turns a wrong mini-whiteboard answer into instant diagnosis, enabling repair of a single atom rather than reteaching a whole lesson.
quotes: Instead of seeing one big skill, I now see thirty tiny, independent concepts and routines.
A lethal mutation is an idea or a practice that is prompted by sound scientific evidence, but is implemented in a way that reduces, or even completely negates, its effectiveness.
You slow down so you can go faster later. When you spend the time to ensure every single atom is 'automated' in the student's long-term memory, something incredible happens.
You're standing at the front of the room watching a low-attaining student solve high-level GCSE problems with total independence because they aren't fighting with the basics.
Because I have the 'X-ray' of the topic, my feedback is instant and precise. I'm not 'reteaching the lesson'; I'm 'repairing the atom.'
